title: Mass conversions: kg, g, mg, micrograms and nanograms
blurb: Convert confidently between kg, g, mg, micrograms and nanograms, knowing which way the point moves and why a mg/microgram slip is a thousandfold error.
question: A person is prescribed digoxin 62.5 micrograms. The stock is labelled in milligrams. What is the dose in milligrams, and which way does the decimal point move?

teach.body: Metric mass units are linked by factors of 1000: 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 g = 1000 mg, 1 mg = 1000 micrograms, 1 microgram = 1000 nanograms. Plain English: each step down the ladder makes the number 1000 times bigger, because the unit is 1000 times smaller. The amount of drug never changes; only the label on the number does.

teach.caption: Going DOWN the ladder (big unit to small) multiply by 1000. Going UP (small to big) divide by 1000.

teach.h: Which way does the point move?
teach.caption: Sense check: the smaller the unit, the more of them you need, so the number must get bigger.

items: Staff nurse Tomasz Nowak checks a prescription for digoxin 62.5 micrograms. The stock is labelled in mg.
Direction: micrograms to mg is small unit to big unit, so divide by 1000.
62.5 ÷ 1000: move the point three places left = 0.0625 mg.
Sense check: 1000 micrograms make 1 mg, so 62.5 micrograms must be well under 1 mg.
He writes 0.0625 mg with a leading zero, and keeps "micrograms" in full on any record.

teach.text: mg and micrograms are 1000 times apart. Reading "micrograms" as "mg" gives a dose 1000 times too large. That is why micrograms and nanograms are written in full and the abbreviation "mcg" or "µg" is avoided: a handwritten µ can look like m. On Part A, answers in micrograms go in a number-only box with "micrograms" printed after it.

items.label: g in 1 kg; mg in 1 g; micrograms in 1 mg
size of the error if mg and micrograms are confused

teach.body: To jump two rungs, multiply or divide by 1000 twice (by 1000000). 0.002 g to micrograms: g to mg gives 2 mg, then mg to micrograms gives 2000 micrograms. Doing one rung at a time and writing the unit at every step stops you stopping halfway.

items: kg, g, mg, micrograms, nanograms: each step is x or ÷ 1000.
Big to small: multiply (point right 3). Small to big: divide (point left 3).
mg vs micrograms is a thousandfold error: write micrograms in full.
Two rungs = two steps of 1000; write the unit at each step.
Answers in micrograms are typed as numbers only, with no commas.

summary: You can now move up and down the kg, g, mg, microgram and nanogram ladder in steps of 1000, choose the direction by asking whether the unit is getting bigger or smaller, and recognise a mg/microgram confusion as a thousandfold error.

whyNot.0: Moved the point two places; g to mg is x 1000 (three places).
whyNot.1: Moved the point four places; g to mg is three places.
whyNot.3: Divided by 1000; going from a big unit to a small one you multiply.

A.why: mg to micrograms: x 1000. 0.15 x 1000 = 150 micrograms.

whyNot.1: Moved the point two places instead of three.
whyNot.2: Moved the point four places instead of three.
whyNot.3: Moved the point one place; mg to micrograms is x 1000.

A.q: Convert 450 mg to grams. Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
A.why: mg to g: ÷ 1000. 450 ÷ 1000 = 0.45 g. Sense check: less than 1000 mg must be less than 1 g.

whyNot.0: Divided by 100; mg to g is ÷ 1000.
whyNot.1: Divided by 10; mg to g is ÷ 1000.
whyNot.2: Divided by 10000; mg to g is three places left, not four.

B.q: A woman in early pregnancy is prescribed folic acid 400 micrograms. How many milligrams is this? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Divided by 100 instead of 1000: a tenfold overdose.
whyNot.2: Divided by 10000; micrograms to mg is ÷ 1000.

B.q: A person on an acute mental health ward is prescribed haloperidol 1.5 mg. How many micrograms is this?
B.why: mg to micrograms: x 1000. 1.5 x 1000 = 1500 micrograms (typed without a comma).

whyNot.1: Multiplied by 100; mg to micrograms is x 1000.
whyNot.2: Multiplied by 10000; mg to micrograms is x 1000.
whyNot.3: Multiplied by 10; mg to micrograms is x 1000.

B.q: An adult on a surgical ward is prescribed flucloxacillin 0.5 g four times a day. How many milligrams is this in 24 hours?
B.why: 0.5 g = 500 mg. 500 mg x 4 = 2000 mg in 24 hours.

whyNot.0: Converted 0.5 g to 50 mg; g to mg is x 1000.
whyNot.1: This is one dose; four doses are given in 24 hours.
whyNot.3: Converted 0.5 g to 5000 mg; g to mg is x 1000.

C.q: A dose of 0.5 micrograms is prescribed. How many nanograms is this?
C.why: Micrograms to nanograms: x 1000. 0.5 x 1000 = 500 nanograms.

whyNot.0: Multiplied by 100; micrograms to nanograms is x 1000.
whyNot.2: Multiplied by 10000; micrograms to nanograms is x 1000.
whyNot.3: Divided by 1000; going down to a smaller unit you multiply.

C.why: g to mg: 0.002 x 1000 = 2 mg. mg to micrograms: 2 x 1000 = 2000 micrograms.

whyNot.0: Stopped after g to mg (2 mg) and wrote the wrong unit.
whyNot.1: Multiplied by 100000; g to micrograms is x 1000000.
whyNot.2: Multiplied by 1000 three times; g to micrograms is two steps.

C.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia receives magnesium sulfate at 1 g per hour. How many milligrams does she receive in 4 hours?
C.why: 1 g per hour x 4 hours = 4 g. 4 g x 1000 = 4000 mg.

whyNot.0: Converted 1 g to 100 mg; g to mg is x 1000.
whyNot.1: Converted 1 g to 10000 mg; g to mg is x 1000.
whyNot.2: Divided 1000 by 4; the hours multiply the dose.

reteach.title: Bigger unit, smaller number
reteach.question: If you swap pound coins for pennies, do you end up with more coins or fewer?

blocks.body: Converting to a smaller unit is like swapping pound coins for pennies: the value is the same, but you hold many more of them. Grams to milligrams, or milligrams to micrograms, works the same way, except the rate is 1000 to 1. So when the unit gets smaller, the number gets 1000 times bigger; when the unit gets bigger, the number gets 1000 times smaller.

blocks.text: If your answer in micrograms is smaller than the number in mg, the point has gone the wrong way.

explain.body: kg, g, mg, micrograms, nanograms, each rung 1000 times the next. Two rungs apart is 1000 x 1000 = 1000000.

test.q: How many micrograms are in 1 g?
test.why: 1 g = 1000 mg, and each mg = 1000 micrograms: 1000 x 1000 = 1000000 micrograms.

whyNot.0: This is micrograms in 1 mg; grams are one more rung up.

explain.body: Going to a smaller unit, multiply by 1000: move the point three places right, adding zeros if needed.

whyNot.0: Moved the point two places; x 1000 is three places.
whyNot.1: Moved the point four places; x 1000 is three places.
whyNot.2: Moved the point one place; x 1000 is three places.

explain.body: Going to a bigger unit, divide by 1000: move the point three places left and add a leading zero if the answer is below 1.

test.q: Convert 2500 micrograms to milligrams. Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Divided by 100; micrograms to mg is ÷ 1000.
whyNot.2: Divided by 10000; micrograms to mg is ÷ 1000.
whyNot.3: Divided by 10; micrograms to mg is ÷ 1000.

explain.text: A dose written in micrograms and read as mg is 1000 times too large. Check the unit word, not just the number.

test.q: A prescription for 125 micrograms is misread as 125 mg. How many times larger is the misread dose? Write your answer as a whole number.
test.why: 125 mg = 125000 micrograms, which is 1000 x 125 micrograms.

whyNot.0: mg and micrograms are one rung apart, which is a factor of 1000.
whyNot.1: A factor of 10 is a one-place decimal slip, not a unit slip.
whyNot.3: That is the factor between g and micrograms, two rungs apart.
